## Why Visualize Data?

- Quick overview of the data
- Spot patterns, outliers, or errors
- Invite the reader

---

### Why Visualize Data?

![Figure 5.15 Catterplot](../../images/catterplot.jpg) 


---


## Different types of graphs in JASP
- Distribution plots (basic plots)
  - Frequency plot when nominal
  - Histogram when scale/ordinal

- Correlation plots (basic plots)
- Scatter plots (customizable plots)
- Raincloud plots


---

## Boxplots: Visualizing Spread and Outliers {.smaller}

- Shows median, quartiles, and outliers
- Useful for comparing groups

![Figure 5.9 Boxplots](../../images/figure-5-9.jpg) 

## Raincloud plots: Boxplots + Raw Data {.smaller}

![Figure 5.11 Raincloud plots](../../images/figure-5-11.jpg) 

---

## Best Practices in Data Visualization

- Use clear labels and titles
- Avoid unnecessary 3D effects
- Choose appropriate scales
- Check for misleading representations


---


## Critically Assess Graphs

- Are axes labelled (variable, units)?
- Are axes broken/equally spaced?
- Are error bars (e.g., confidence intervals) included where relevant?

---

### Critically Assess Graphs
```{r, echo=FALSE}
set.seed(123)

A <- rnorm(10, mean = 5, sd = 3)
B <- rnorm(10, mean = 7, sd = 3)
means <- c(mean(A), mean(B))
ses   <- c(sd(A)/sqrt(length(A)), sd(B)/sqrt(length(B)))
tcrit <- qt(0.975, df = c(length(A)-1, length(B)-1))

# Bad: no axis labels
bp <- barplot(means, names.arg = c("SPSS", "JASP"),
              ylab = "Exam performance",
              col = c("skyblue", "orange"), ylim = c(0, 10), axes = FALSE)
```




## Scale Matters
```{r, echo=FALSE}

# Bad: no axis labels
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
bp <- barplot(means, names.arg = c("SPSS", "JASP"),
              ylab = "Grade (0-10)",
              col = c("skyblue", "orange"), ylim = c(0, 10), axes = FALSE)
axis(2)

bp <- barplot(means, names.arg = c("SPSS", "JASP"),
              ylab = "Grade (0-100)",
              col = c("skyblue", "orange"), ylim = c(0, 10), axes = FALSE)
# Add error bars
# arrows(x0 = bp, y0 = means - ses, x1 = bp, y1 = means + ses,
#        angle = 90, code = 3, length = 0.06, lwd = 1.5)
axis(2, labels = seq(90, 100, 2), at = seq(0, 10, by =2))
```


## Error Bars!
```{r, echo=FALSE}

# Bad: no axis labels
bp <- barplot(means, names.arg = c("SPSS", "JASP"),
              ylab = "Grade (0-10)",
              col = c("skyblue", "orange"), ylim = c(0, 10), axes = FALSE)
axis(2)
arrows(x0 = bp, y0 = means - ses*tcrit, x1 = bp, y1 = means + ses*tcrit,
        angle = 90, code = 3, length = 0.06, lwd = 1.5)

```




# Leaving Data Out {.section}

## 28 January 1986 {.smaller}

The night before the *Challenger* launch, engineers argued about whether the cold would damage the rubber O-ring seals on the booster rockets.

They reviewed the damage recorded on previous flights, plotted against the temperature at launch.

Tomorrow's forecast: **31°F (-0.5°C)**. Should they launch?

## The evidence they reviewed {.smaller}

```{r, echo=FALSE}
source("../../_setup.R")
challenger <- read.csv(datasetsPath("2026/Challenger.csv"))
damaged    <- subset(challenger, Any_Damage == "Yes")

par(cex = 1.0, cex.lab = 1.1)
plot(damaged$Temperature_F, damaged$Damaged_ORings,
     pch = 19, cex = 2, col = "darkred", las = 1, bty = "n",
     xlab = "Temperature at launch (F)", ylab = "Damaged O-rings",
     xlim = c(50, 85), ylim = c(0, 6),
     main = "Flights that suffered O-ring damage")
```

Seven flights, no obvious pattern. Cold does not look dangerous.

## The flights that were left off {.smaller}

```{r, echo=FALSE}
par(cex = 1.0, cex.lab = 1.1)
cols <- ifelse(challenger$Any_Damage == "Yes", "darkred", "darkgreen")

plot(challenger$Temperature_F, challenger$Damaged_ORings,
     pch = 19, cex = 2, col = cols, las = 1, bty = "n",
     xlab = "Temperature at launch (F)", ylab = "Damaged O-rings",
     xlim = c(50, 85), ylim = c(0, 6),
     main = "All 23 previous flights")

legend("topright", legend = c("damage", "no damage"),
       pch = 19, col = c("darkred", "darkgreen"), bty = "n", cex = 0.9)
```

The sixteen flights with **no** damage were the whole argument: they were the warm ones.

## Off the edge of the data {.smaller}

```{r, echo=FALSE}
par(cex = 1.0, cex.lab = 1.1)
fit <- glm(cbind(Damaged_ORings, 6 - Damaged_ORings) ~ Temperature_F,
           family = binomial, data = challenger)

tempGrid <- seq(30, 85, 0.5)
pred     <- predict(fit, newdata = data.frame(Temperature_F = tempGrid),
                    type = "response")

plot(tempGrid, pred, type = "l", lwd = 3, col = "darkblue", las = 1, bty = "n",
     xlab = "Temperature at launch (F)", ylab = "P(O-ring damaged)",
     ylim = c(0, 1), main = "Fitted model, extrapolated to launch day")

points(challenger$Temperature_F, challenger$Damaged_ORings / 6,
       pch = 19, cex = 1.5, col = cols)

abline(v = 31, lwd = 3, lty = 2, col = "darkred")
text(31, 0.55, "launch day\n31 F", pos = 4, col = "darkred", cex = 0.9)
abline(v = min(challenger$Temperature_F), lwd = 2, lty = 3)
text(min(challenger$Temperature_F), 0.15, "coldest\nprior flight", pos = 4, cex = 0.8)
```

## What the plot could not say {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
- With only the damaged flights: $r = -0.58$, $p = .17$. With all of them: $r = -0.64$, $p = .001$
- The correlation barely changes. What changes is whether you can *see* it
- Launch day was 22°F colder than anything in the data. No plot can tell you what happens out there
:::

<small>The engineers did recommend against launching; they were overruled. Tufte's well-known "the chart caused the disaster" reading (*Visual Explanations*, 1997) is disputed, see Robison et al. (2002). Data: Dalal, Fowlkes & Hoadley (1989), via `faraway::orings`.</small>
